title: The Register of the Gods
subtitle: Hierarchical Clustering · hclust + cutree + summarise
story: You are an apprentice to the keeper at the Temple of the Gods. The keeper died of a fever last month and with him were lost two important registers: which offering each shrine takes, and which god each shrine serves. According to custom, a temple whose keeper dies is closed forever — its fires never relit — unless the registers exist. You have until midday, when the sun is at its zenith and the shafts of light through the roof stand straight and touch the altar, to rebuild them. The evidence is still here — the residues in every vessel, the figures standing in every niche. Rebuild both registers, light the ring of fires at the altar so the temple is seen to be kept, and then cross the canopy bridge to the temple beyond and tell them the registers are in hand.

done.title: The practical register is whole
done.body: Every shrine, every offering, in your own hand — and two of them filed against the stone in the inner vault, because the vessels said so and the stone was only recording where things happen to stand. It is the smaller of the two books and the easier one. Outside, the shadow under the parapet has pulled in almost to nothing.

escapeDone.title: Not closed
escapeDone.body: Three groups, and the last one closes. Whatever the figures in those niches have been saying to each other for four hundred years, you have finally heard it. You tip the one flame you carried up out of the dark into the channel and it runs the whole ring, basin to basin, with the sun standing straight overhead and the whole green roof of the forest flat below. He taught you after all — he just did it by leaving everything exactly where it was.

worldPlatePrompt: A world-bible establishing plate for a LIVING, KEPT jungle temple, deep in rainforest, at harsh equatorial midday. This sanctuary was tended every day until a month ago, when its keeper died: it is swept, maintained and in use — NOT a ruin. Nothing has collapsed, there is no rubble, nothing is growing through the floor, and the forest is cut hard back and stops at the wall. One frame holding the whole world's vocabulary: massive warm honey-and-ochre limestone masonry, close-jointed and clean, its carved faces still crisp and still holding traces of painted plaster; a gallery of shallow shrine niches cut along the wall, each hung with a single banner of strong flat colour; small carved stone and clay votive figures standing in tidy rows on wiped niche ledges; lamps with trimmed wicks and shallow offering bowls set square before them, recently used and now cold; stoppered resin jars stacked in order along the floor; a low rough service crawl-way cut behind the wall at floor level — the one unfinished thing, its dust worn into a smooth path by daily passing; and hard white shafts of sunlight falling straight down through openings in the canopy far above, striking the floor in sharp bright pools. LIGHT: harsh, flat and OVERHEAD, high noon, hard-edged shafts and short shadows. Deliberately NOT golden hour, NOT dusk, NOT dawn, NOT lamplit — no warm amber wash anywhere, no firelight, no brass glow. PALETTE: RICH AND LUMINOUS, not grey and not washed-out — warm honey stone, deep wet greens in the forest beyond, real blue in the sky and in the shadows, clear water. The nine banners are the only PURE, fully saturated colour in the frame and nothing else competes with them for chroma, but everything else is still full of colour and light. Humid air, drifting spore and dust in the light shafts, water beading on stone. Painterly, cinematic, subtle film grain. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no readable writing, no signage, no UI.

A hard bar of overhead noon sun falls across the ledge, with deep warm shade to either side; a lit clay lamp and a shallow offering bowl sit before the figures. debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: Everything in this scenario was one technique in costume: hierarchical clustering — sorting things into a nested tree of groups by how alike their measurements are. Here is what you actually did, with the story taken back off.

plannedHotspots.label: The unlabelled stores
plannedHotspots.note: The season's offerings, every jar unlabelled — this is WHY rung 1 matters (the keeper drew for sister shrines from one jar). Flavour + motivation; no answer here.
plannedHotspots.body:
Jars to the roof, and not one label on any of them. What each shrine actually took is still crusted inside its own vessels, though, and every one has been scraped and measured — six substances, shrine by shrine.

That is the whole of the practical register: shrines that took the same offering leave the same residues, so shrines that belong together are the ones whose six numbers sit close together.

pick.prompt: The keeper drew for sister shrines from one jar, so two shrines that took the same offering left the same residues behind in their vessels. Using temple_votive_residues, measure how far every other shrine's residues sit from Ninestep's, plot that distance for all eight shrines, assign your plot to p, and click the shrine that sits nearest to Ninestep.
pick.plotCode:
dm <- as.matrix(dist(temple_votive_residues[, 3:8]))
rownames(dm) <- colnames(dm) <- temple_votive_residues$shrine
near <- data.frame(shrine = colnames(dm), distance = as.numeric(dm["Ninestep", ]))
near <- near[near$shrine != "Ninestep", ]
p <- ggplot(near, aes(x = distance, y = shrine)) + geom_point(size = 3)
pick.hint: The six residue measurements are columns 3 to 8. dist() on those columns gives every pairwise distance at once — name the rows with shrine, take the Ninestep row, and plot it.

feedback.correct: Correct — noted: Ninestep's sister shrine is Longshadow. Their six residues sit 3.2 apart, where the next nearest shrine, Deepwell, is 5.7 away.
wrong: Every shrine is six residue measurements. Two shrines are sisters when those six numbers sit closest together, so work out the distance from Ninestep to each of the other eight and compare them.
dist(temple_votive_residues[, 3:8]) gives all the pairwise distances in one go. Put the shrine names on it with rownames(), pull out the Ninestep row, and plot distance against shrine.
Three shrines sit close to Ninestep and five sit far away. Among the close three, one is clearly nearer than the other two — that is the sister, not merely a near neighbour.

ladderPlain.text: In the first puzzle you measured how far apart the shrines were, using all six residue measurements at once rather than one at a time, and found the shrine whose residues sat closest to Ninestep's. Every puzzle after this one was built on those pairwise distances.

In the second puzzle you turned those distances into a tree, cut the tree into three families of shrines, and took one average for each family — the mean beeswax — so you could say which family the last block of wax belonged to.

In the third puzzle you added the sealed cell's bowl, which carries no name, to the nine known shrines and clustered all ten together, so that the cell's own residues decided which family it joined rather than where in the temple it was found.

In the last puzzle you clustered the shrines once more and set each shrine's family against the wing column, which records where that shrine stands in the temple today. For seven of the nine the two agree. For Deepwell and Palewall they disagree, and it is the residues that settle it: a shrine's offering follows the god it serves, while its wing only records where it has ended up. That is how you knew those two were the ones that had been moved.

escapeBrief: To get out you sorted the nine shrines into their three families a second time, with no data table and no console — using only the figures carved on each shrine's plate. It is the same judgement the clustering made for you in the puzzles: deciding what belongs with what by comparing every shrine against every other, rather than by which room you found it in.
